title: Shrey Mudgal
text: Hello! I’m currently a Master of Data Science student at the University of British Columbia.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Orientation day on campus.



Orientation was excellent. We received a comprehensive overview of what the next 10 months would look like, met several alumni who shared their tips and advice, and had the chance to ask them questions directly. There was also an informative session on maintaining mental well-being, and we were introduced to all faculty members along with guidance on how and where to reach out for support. What surprised me most was how approachable the faculty were; you could walk up and speak with anyone, and one of the senior director holds office hours where you can discuss the program in general.
The first week was hectic, especially DSCI 551, which threw a lot at us right away. I stayed diligent, putting in significant time each day to complete the assignments, and that effort paid off; I finished all the required work by Saturday afternoon and was able to relax for the rest of the weekend.
Heading into week 3, I’m feeling a bit nervous. A lot of material has been covered, there’s a great deal to retain, and balancing the upcoming assignments, labs, and quizzes will be challenging.

title: Penguin body size, measured in R
text:
Data: Palmer Penguins.
Citation: Horst, Hill and Gorman (2020), doi:10.5281/zenodo.3960218. The data is released under CC0.
Three species turn up in this data: Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo. I want to compare them on two measurements, body mass in grams and flipper length in millimetres, and then check how tightly the variables move with each other. The palmerpenguins package contains the data file inside the package.
I load the packages first. This chunk is ran quietly: palmerpenguins masks two objects from the datasets package when it loads and prints a note about it, and that note is noise in the middle of a page.

library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

The table holds 344 penguins. Two of them are missing both measurements, so I remove those rows and keep 342. I drop the bill columns since I am not using them.

penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g), !is.na(flipper_length_mm)) |>
  select(species, island, sex, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)

nrow(penguins_clean)

[1] 342

head(penguins_clean)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  species island    sex    flipper_length_mm body_mass_g
  <fct>   <fct>     <fct>              <int>       <int>
1 Adelie  Torgersen male                 181        3750
2 Adelie  Torgersen female               186        3800
3 Adelie  Torgersen female               195        3250
4 Adelie  Torgersen female               193        3450
5 Adelie  Torgersen male                 190        3650
6 Adelie  Torgersen female               181        3625


Body mass splits the species more sharply than I expected. Adelie and Chinstrap average almost the same, around 3.7 kg, while Gentoo come in near 5.1 kg, roughly 1.4 kg heavier. Flipper length tells a similar story, with Gentoo at about 217 mm against 190 mm for Adelie.

penguins_clean |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g),
    sd_mass_g = sd(body_mass_g),
    mean_flipper_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)

The boxplot shows how much overlap there is. Adelie and Chinstrap sit on top of each other with a lot of spread, and Gentoo are shifted well clear of both.

ggplot(penguins_clean, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Body mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







Figure 1: Body mass of penguins by species.





Flipper length and body mass are strongly related, with a correlation near 0.87. Longer flippers go with heavier birds. However, this requires further analysis as the metric relation I used here is quite simple.

cor(penguins_clean$flipper_length_mm, penguins_clean$body_mass_g)

title: Penguin body size, measured in Python
text:
Data: Palmer Penguins.
Citation: Horst, Hill and Gorman (2020), doi:10.5281/zenodo.3960218. The data is released under CC0.
Three species turn up in this data: Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo. I want to compare them on two measurements, body mass in grams and flipper length in millimetres, and then check how tightly the variables move with each other. The Python port of the R palmerpenguins package contains the data file inside the package.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

The table holds 344 penguins. Two of them are missing both measurements, so I remove those rows and keep 342. I drop the bill columns since I am not using them.

penguins = load_penguins()

clean = penguins.dropna(subset=["body_mass_g", "flipper_length_mm"])[
    ["species", "island", "sex", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]
]

Body mass splits the species more sharply than I expected. Adelie and Chinstrap average almost the same, around 3.7 kg, while Gentoo come in near 5.1 kg, roughly 1.4 kg heavier. Flipper length tells a similar story, with Gentoo at about 217 mm against 190 mm for Adelie.

summary = (
    clean.groupby("species")
    .agg(
        n=("body_mass_g", "size"),
        mean_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "mean"),
        sd_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "std"),
        mean_flipper_mm=("flipper_length_mm", "mean"),
    )
    .round(1)
)
summary["n"] = summary["n"].astype(int)

title: About
text: I earned my bachelor’s degree in computer science from Delhi Technological University. I then moved to the United States, where I completed a master’s degree in information systems. My professional journey began as a data analyst at a manufacturing company, where I applied data science techniques including time series forecasting, predictive modeling, and machine learning. I later joined Discover (Capital One), where I held roles as a business intelligence analyst and subsequently as a software/data engineer.

Why data science
Throughout my career, I found myself increasingly drawn back to the data science work I had enjoyed earlier on. Recognizing this, I decided to pivot by enrolling in UBC’s Master of Data Science program. My goal is to transition into a full-time data scientist role.
